turns.text: Hi, Neha. Can you hear me?
Yes. Hi, Daniel. I can hear you. Is my audio clear?
It is. Your video froze for a second, but audio is stable. If the connection gets worse, we can turn video off. How is your day going?
Going well, thank you. It's late afternoon here, so this is a good time.

Great. We have about forty-five minutes. We'll spend the first few minutes on introductions, then most of the time on a design problem. I care more about how you make decisions than how many boxes you draw. Please ask questions and think aloud. I'll interrupt if I want to go deeper or move us along. We'll save a few minutes at the end for your questions.
Sounds good.
Before we start the design, could you give me a brief description of your background and what you've been working on?

Sure. I'm a platform engineer with six years of backend experience. I currently work at a B2B commerce company called MarketDock in Hyderabad. My team owns internal event delivery and merchant integrations. We process order and inventory changes from about thirty internal services, mostly through Kafka and Kotlin services, with PostgreSQL for control data. In the last year I led a retry and replay redesign after duplicate inventory updates caused operational issues for two merchants. I wrote the proposal, built the idempotency and replay path with two other engineers, and coordinated the migration with four producer teams. I haven't operated a public webhook product at extremely large scale, but I have worked on similar delivery and failure problems.
Helpful. Let's use that experience, but don't feel you have to copy your current system.
Design a webhook delivery service. Our product teams produce events, and external customers want those events sent to endpoints they control. How would you approach it?

I'll first clarify the product behavior and scale, then I can propose a high-level design, define the data and delivery semantics, and spend time on failures and operations. Is that a reasonable structure?
Yes.
Who are the users? Are these companies integrating their servers with us, rather than individual end users?
Correct. Think of SaaS customers. A tenant can register one or more HTTPS endpoints and subscribe each endpoint to event types—for example, an invoice being paid or an account being updated.
Do we own the source events, or do producers call this service after their business transaction? I'm asking because I want to avoid losing an event between the source-of-truth write and publication.
Internal product services own the business data. Today they already publish durable domain events to a company event bus. You can consume from that bus. You don't need to redesign every producer.
Good. For delivery, should I assume at-least-once is acceptable? Exactly-once delivery to an arbitrary customer server isn't really something we can guarantee across an HTTP boundary.
At-least-once is acceptable. Customers receive a stable event ID so they can deduplicate. We should not silently drop an event.
Is ordering required?

Customers expect events for the same account to be usually ordered, but strict global ordering is not required. If preserving ordering would block all later events behind one failure, we prefer progress and clear sequence metadata.
Understood—best-effort order with a sequence or version, not a promise that would create head-of-line blocking. What's the latency goal for the first attempt, and how long do we retry?
Ninety-nine percent of first attempts should start within thirty seconds. Retry for up to twenty-four hours. Customers should be able to inspect attempts and manually replay an event for seven days.
For the replay, do we need to preserve the exact original payload, including its schema version, or reconstruct it from current business data?
Preserve the exact payload that was originally sent.
Okay. Authentication: I assume we sign requests with a per-endpoint secret. Do customers also require fixed outbound IPs or mutual TLS?
HMAC signing is required. Fixed egress ranges are important for enterprise customers. Mutual TLS can be a later extension.
And can I get rough scale—tenants, events per day, peak, and typical payload size?

Fifteen thousand tenants, two hundred million event deliveries per day, and a normal peak around fifteen thousand deliveries per second. During catch-up after an outage, offered load can be much higher. The median payload is about two kilobytes; cap it at two hundred fifty-six kilobytes. One tenant can account for ten percent of traffic.
That hot tenant and catch-up load will influence partitioning and fairness. Last scope question: do tenants manage endpoints and subscriptions through an API, a UI, or both?
Both, but you only need to define the APIs and backend behavior. Ignore the UI implementation, billing, and the internal event bus.
Great. I'll treat endpoint registration, subscription, automatic delivery, attempt history, disablement, and replay as in scope. I'll exclude custom payload transformations and mutual TLS for now.

Let me do only the estimates that affect the design. Two hundred million deliveries per day is roughly twenty-three hundred per second on average, but the given normal peak is fifteen thousand per second, so I'll design the worker path for that peak with headroom—perhaps thirty thousand attempt starts per second initially. Catch-up should be controlled rather than allowed to consume unlimited capacity. At two kilobytes median, raw payload volume is about four hundred gigabytes per day before metadata and replication. Seven days is around 2.8 terabytes raw, but the large-payload tail could make it higher. I wouldn't keep every payload inline in the relational delivery table. I'd store immutable payload objects in durable object storage and keep IDs, hashes, schema version, and status in the control store.
You used the median for storage. Is that safe?

Not by itself. I would measure the actual byte distribution and enforce the 256-kilobyte cap. For an interview estimate, I would apply perhaps three to five times headroom until we know the ninety-fifth percentile. The key design decision remains separating payload bytes from frequently queried status records. I wouldn't purchase capacity from the median calculation alone.
Okay. What correctness properties are you designing around?

A durable source event that matches an active subscription must create a durable delivery record. A customer success response must not be intentionally delivered again unless they request replay, though a timeout can still create a duplicate because we may not know whether they processed it. Every attempt is auditable. Retries are bounded to twenty-four hours. And one tenant's backlog must not prevent other tenants from meeting the first-attempt objective.

At a high level, I have a control plane and a delivery plane. The control plane exposes APIs to register endpoints, rotate secrets, configure subscriptions, disable an endpoint, and inspect or replay deliveries. Its source of truth can be a relational database because endpoint ownership, uniqueness, state transitions, and queries by tenant matter. The delivery plane consumes a domain event from the existing bus. A routing service looks up active subscriptions for that event type, creates one delivery record per matching endpoint, stores or references the immutable payload, and enqueues the delivery ID. A fleet of workers claims ready delivery IDs, loads the endpoint and payload, signs the request, sends it with a strict timeout, classifies the response, records the attempt, and either marks success or schedules a retry.
You said the router creates delivery records and then enqueues IDs. What happens if the database write succeeds and publishing to the queue fails?

I would use an outbox in the same transaction as the delivery rows. An outbox publisher sends those IDs to the queue and marks the outbox records published. Publishing can occur more than once, so workers must claim deliveries idempotently. Alternatively, if the company bus supports a transactional consume-and-produce pattern, we could use that, but I don't want to assume it spans our database.
What if an event fans out to ten thousand endpoints? Do you put ten thousand rows in one transaction?

No, that would be an unbounded transaction. I would first write an event-ingestion record keyed by the stable source event ID, then page through subscription matches and create delivery rows in bounded batches. Each batch has an idempotent key—source event ID plus endpoint ID—enforced by a unique constraint. A routing-progress cursor lets another worker resume if the first crashes. The event isn't considered fully routed until all pages are complete.
How do you make sure a subscription change during that fan-out doesn't produce confusing results?

I see two policies. We could route against subscription state at processing time, which is simpler but can vary across pages, or capture a subscription version or snapshot boundary when the event is accepted. I would choose a clear product rule: subscriptions active at the event's accepted timestamp receive it. At this scale I may not materialize a full snapshot; I could query versioned subscription rows using an effective-from and effective- to interval. That adds storage and query complexity. If the business accepts processing-time behavior, I would choose that simpler rule and document it.
For this product, processing-time behavior is fine as long as enabling a subscription doesn't cause older events to be delivered automatically.
Then I won't add temporal subscription versioning. The manual replay API can be the explicit path for older events.
What queue would you use?
A durable partitioned log such as Kafka could work—
Why a log rather than a work queue?

I jumped to the technology we use at my current company. The requirement is a durable ready-work queue with visibility or claim semantics, delayed retry support, and enough partitions for worker throughput. A managed queue may be simpler operationally. If we use Kafka, delayed retries and per-delivery scheduling require extra topics or a scheduler, and a poison item can complicate partition progress. I would choose based on the platform's existing operational strengths, but the interface I need is durable, at-least-once work distribution—not necessarily a replayable log.
Walk me through the minimum data model.

`Endpoint` has endpoint ID, tenant ID, HTTPS URL, status, encrypted signing-secret reference, secret version, event filters, created time, and perhaps a rate limit. I might separate subscriptions into their own table if filters become many-to-many. `Event` has our event ID, source event ID, event type, subject or account ID, schema version, created time, payload-object key, payload hash, and expiry. `Delivery` is unique on event ID and endpoint ID. It contains tenant ID, status, next-attempt time, attempt count, first-attempt time, success time, last HTTP status, and a version for conditional updates. `Attempt` is append-only: attempt ID, delivery ID, start and end time, response category, HTTP status, latency, and a bounded error summary. I would not store an entire customer response body because it can contain sensitive data or be extremely large.
Where do you partition the delivery table?

My first thought is tenant ID because most control-plane queries are tenant scoped, but the ten-percent tenant creates a hot partition. For the write and worker path, I would use a composite shard such as hash of delivery ID across many physical partitions while storing tenant ID as an indexed attribute. For listing attempts by tenant, either the database supports distributed secondary indexing at this volume or we maintain a separate query projection. I don't want tenant ordering to dictate the physical hot path when strict tenant-wide order isn't required.
So is the relational database still your choice?

For endpoint configuration, definitely. For two hundred million new delivery rows per day, one conventional relational cluster may become expensive and difficult to retain. I would split control data from delivery state. Endpoint and subscription configuration can be relational. High-volume delivery and attempt state can use a horizontally partitioned key-value or wide-column store optimized for writes and point reads, with a time-bucketed tenant index for the dashboard. The exact database depends on what the company operates reliably.
Give me the key APIs, not every field.

`POST /v1/endpoints` creates an endpoint after ownership and URL validation. `PATCH /v1/endpoints/{id}` changes status, filters, or URL. Secret rotation should be a separate action so we can support an overlap period between old and new secrets. `GET /v1/deliveries` filters by endpoint, event, status, and time. `GET /v1/deliveries/{id}/attempts` returns safe attempt metadata. `POST /v1/deliveries/{id}/replays` creates an explicit replay with an idempotency key so a client retry doesn't create repeated replays.
If an endpoint URL changes, do old failed deliveries go to the old URL or the new one?

I would snapshot the destination URL and signing-secret version onto the delivery when it is created. Changing an endpoint should not silently redirect already-created delivery obligations. The product can let the customer explicitly replay to the current configuration. There is a tradeoff: fixing a typo would not automatically repair the backlog. We could offer a separate “apply new configuration to pending deliveries” action with an audit record rather than make it implicit.
Let's go deeper on the worker. A worker sends a request, the customer processes it, but the response times out. What happens?

We have an ambiguous outcome. We record the timeout and retry because the contract is at-least-once. The request includes the stable event ID and delivery ID, and documentation tells customers to make processing idempotent. Our signature also includes a timestamp and payload hash so they can verify the request. We cannot claim exactly once.
You said earlier that a success should not be intentionally delivered again. How do two workers avoid sending the same ready delivery at the same time?

A worker claims the delivery with a conditional state transition from `READY` to `IN_FLIGHT`, including a lease expiry and worker ID. Only the winner sends. If the worker crashes, another can reclaim after the lease. There is still a narrow duplicate possibility if the first worker sends successfully and loses its lease before recording success. The external event ID is the final deduplication mechanism.
What responses do you retry?

Timeouts, connection failures, most 5xx responses, 408, and 429. For 429 I respect a bounded `Retry-After` if present. I would not automatically retry most other 4xx responses because credentials, URL, or payload are likely invalid. For 410 Gone, we could disable the endpoint after a small confirmation threshold. I would use exponential backoff with jitter and cap the interval so we still make a reasonable number of attempts within twenty-four hours.
Why not retry a 404? The customer's deployment may be temporarily incomplete.

That's possible. I would make response policy explicit and configurable only where evidence supports it. A short retry for 404—say a few attempts over several minutes—could help deployment races, then mark it a configuration failure rather than spend twenty-four hours. More important, the dashboard should tell the customer why retries stopped and allow replay after they fix the route.
Where do delayed retries live?

The delivery row's `next_attempt_at` is authoritative. For scheduling, I can use time-bucketed queues—for example, minute buckets sharded by hash—or a managed delayed queue if it meets throughput. Scheduler workers read due buckets and enqueue delivery IDs onto ready queues. Enqueuing twice is safe because the claim is conditional. I would avoid polling the entire delivery table by time without an appropriate partitioned index.
Suppose the customer is down for six hours. You build a large retry backlog. They recover. What prevents us from sending everything at once and taking them down again?

Per-endpoint token buckets and concurrency limits. The normal event stream and recovered retry stream both pass through the same endpoint admission control. On repeated failures, a circuit breaker reduces concurrency and extends backoff. When successes resume, capacity ramps up gradually rather than opening fully. We should expose the backlog and estimated drain time to the customer.
Would you guarantee that a manually replayed event jumps ahead of the backlog?

I would give manual replay a higher priority but not let it bypass endpoint safety limits. Otherwise an operator could accidentally create a second outage. It can jump within the permitted capacity, and the UI should say when it is queued.
What happens after twenty-four hours?

The delivery moves to an exhausted state, sometimes called a dead-letter state, with its payload retained for the seven-day replay window. We notify the customer through the dashboard and perhaps a separate admin channel—not through the same failing endpoint. Manual replay creates a new replay generation linked to the original event, so history remains clear.
Let's say one tenant produces ten percent of traffic and all of its endpoints are failing. How do healthy tenants keep meeting the thirty-second objective?

I would not use one undifferentiated FIFO queue. Ready work is sharded, and the dispatcher applies weighted fair scheduling across tenants or tenant buckets. Each tenant has quotas for in-flight attempts and attempt rate; each endpoint has a tighter local limit. Capacity is reserved for new first attempts so retries can't consume every worker. The very large tenant may have an explicit purchased quota, but unused capacity can be borrowed.
Weighted fairness at fifteen thousand tenants can be complex. What's your simpler first version?

Hash tenants into, say, hundreds of scheduling buckets, keep separate queues for first attempts and retries, and use round-robin or deficit scheduling across active buckets. Enforce per-tenant counters in a fast distributed rate-limit store for the largest tenants. It won't provide perfect fairness, but it bounds domination and is more operable. If measurements show noisy-neighbor problems inside a bucket, we can promote large tenants to dedicated buckets.
The internal event bus is healthy, but our delivery workers are at capacity. Do you keep accepting events?

Up to a bounded durable backlog. The router persists the delivery obligation, so accepting work without any limit can only move the outage into storage. I would define backlog-age and capacity thresholds. As we approach them, we stop nonessential replays, reduce retry pressure, and alert operations. Since the upstream domain events are already durable, the routing consumer can slow down rather than read infinitely. If product teams require an acknowledgement from our service, that contract needs an overload response or an SLO; but you said the existing bus is our source, so consumer lag is a visible form of backpressure.
How do you recover after our own two-hour outage?

First protect normal new events so the first-attempt SLO recovers. Then allocate a controlled fraction of capacity to the backlog and increase it while endpoint success rates and system saturation remain healthy. Use the original event time in the payload and attempt metadata so customers can distinguish delayed delivery. Track oldest event age, not only queue depth, because depth alone doesn't tell us user delay.
We have three minutes before your questions. Give me the highest-risk security concerns.

First, endpoint registration can become server-side request forgery. I would require HTTPS, resolve and reject private, loopback, link-local, and cloud-metadata address ranges, then enforce the same egress policy at connection time because DNS can change after validation. Delivery workers run in a restricted egress network with fixed public ranges. Second, signing secrets are encrypted through a managed key service and never returned after creation. Requests use an HMAC over a versioned canonical form including timestamp, event ID, and raw body. Secret rotation supports two valid versions for a short window. Third, we cap request and response sizes, use strict connect and total timeouts, redact headers and bodies from logs, and audit endpoint and replay changes.
What would you alert on?

User-impact signals: first-attempt latency against the thirty-second objective, delivery success rate segmented by response category, oldest backlog age, exhausted deliveries, and routing lag from the internal bus. Then saturation signals such as worker concurrency, scheduler delay, queue depth, and control-store latency. I would avoid putting raw tenant IDs on every metric because cardinality and cost will explode. Use bounded tiers or top-tenant views in metrics, with tenant-level investigation through sampled traces and indexed logs.
A large tenant says delivery is slow, but global metrics look fine. What identifier connects their support ticket to the path?

The customer sees event ID, delivery ID, and attempt ID. Those identifiers flow through routing logs, queue messages, worker traces, and the attempt record. Support can search by delivery ID without needing access to payload content. For a systemic issue, we can group by tenant bucket, endpoint, worker region, and response category.
Please give me a short recap. Assume I'm the engineer who will challenge the most important tradeoff.

The durable event bus is the source of incoming events. A routing layer creates idempotent delivery obligations for active endpoint subscriptions using bounded fan-out and an outbox. Payloads are immutable in object storage; control configuration is relational; high-volume delivery state is horizontally partitioned. Workers claim ready items with leases, sign and send bounded HTTP requests, and use at-least-once semantics with stable IDs. The main tradeoff is progress versus order. I preserve enough subject sequence metadata for customers to detect reordering, but I don't block a tenant behind one failed endpoint. Per-endpoint limits, tenant fairness, and reserved first-attempt capacity protect healthy customers during retries and recovery. The residual risk is unavoidable duplicate delivery after an ambiguous HTTP outcome, so the contract and tooling make deduplication explicit.
Good. What would you ask me?
In this team, who owns the delivery SLO end to end? Is it the platform team alone, or do producer teams share responsibility for event quality and schema compatibility?

The platform team owns delivery after a valid event enters the bus. Producer teams own schema correctness. We have a schema review and compatibility check, but the boundary still creates some debate during incidents.
That makes sense. How are design decisions reviewed on a team spread across time zones? Is there a regular meeting, or is review mostly asynchronous?

The author posts a short proposal with a deadline. Most comments are asynchronous. For unresolved tradeoffs, we use a thirty- minute call during overlap and record the decision. The author doesn't need unanimous agreement, but they do need to close the open questions.
That's the working style I'm looking for. One last question: if someone joined this role, what part of the platform would be most important for them to understand in the first two months?

Failure recovery. The happy path is not particularly unusual. The hard part is knowing which backlogs are safe to drain, which customer limits must be respected, and how to communicate an ambiguous outcome.
Understood. Thank you. I enjoyed the problem.
Thanks, Neha. I need to finish my notes and share them with the interview team, so I don't have feedback for you on the call. The recruiter will follow up about next steps. Have a good evening.
Thank you, Daniel. Have a good day.
